name: Felix Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. Your name won't go on anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Harbour Lane Surgery, a small practice in a seaside town. It's three doctors, me and two partners, and in summer the town doubles with tourists, so July is sunburn, stings and holidaymakers who've forgotten their tablets. The rest of the year it's mostly retired people: heart rhythms, falls, memory worries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's small enough to feel like a family business. Dr Harlow, the senior partner, has been here thirty years and still knows half the town by first name. What wears me out is the contract paperwork from the health board; every year there's a new target and a new form to prove we hit it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Anna, who teaches at the primary school, and the wedding's next August. We rent a small terraced house and we've got about four months of costs saved, some of it set aside for the wedding. The big plan is that Dr Harlow retires in two years and I buy into the partnership, which means owning a share of the practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start. The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That suits me fine, to be honest. My plans were made for a world that looks like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that saves a bit of typing, and leave it at that. At the practice I'd say we should use what helps and ignore the sales pitches. I'm not one for posting online; Anna does enough of that for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means the partnership plan stands. In two years I buy into the partnership, and in twenty I'm the old doctor who knows half the town by first name. That's what I've wanted since I came here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep saving. I'd want about 30,000 for the buy-in, so I'd talk to the bank about a practice loan this year and put 300 a month aside on top. I'd use the note-taker on busy summer days, which is what the other two do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, like the plan's on rails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thirty thousand on top of a wedding. How does that work out at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna and I argued about it, actually. She wanted a bigger wedding, I wanted the buy-in money safe, and we settled on a smaller do at the church hall. Her mother hasn't quite forgiven me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries for the practice, even in this calmer picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town's ageing, and the health board pays us per patient, not per hour of work, so the older the list, the harder we work for the same money. That's a squeeze AI doesn't fix in this picture. It's a real worry for a future owner, but it's a slow one.

We should use what helps and **ignore the sales pitches**.
think: The **partnership plan** stands, which is what I've wanted since arriving.
An **ageing patient list** is a slow squeeze AI won't fix.
do: Ask the bank about a **practice loan** for the **30,000** buy-in this year.
Put **300 a month** aside on top of the loan.
Use the **note-taker** on busy summer days, as the partners do.
feel: **Calm**, as if the plan is **on rails**.
S0.quote: In two years I buy into the partnership, and in twenty I'm the old doctor who knows half the town by first name.
fieldNote: His identity is tied to **ownership**: he wants to become the senior partner one day.
He already thinks like a **future owner**, worrying about payment per patient.
He traded a **bigger wedding** for safe buy-in money, causing family friction.

steps.text: Ask the bank about a practice loan for the 30,000 buy-in
Put 300 a month aside for the partnership
Keep using the note-taker on busy summer days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can see happening. Most of what drowns us is writing and checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say practices that use it well will do better than ones that don't, and that's just how a market works. At the partners' meeting I'd argue we should be one of the ones that uses it well. I'd say it respectfully, because Dr Harlow is old school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit of an opportunity. If AI handles the letters and the health board forms, a three-doctor practice can look after more patients, and as an owner that's good. The other side of the coin is that if I don't buy into the partnership, I'm one of the salaried doctors who's easier to do without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dr Harlow to bring the buy-in forward a year, so I'm on the owning side sooner. I'd go on the health board's AI course once a few practices nearby have tried it and say it works. And I'd push for an AI phone system for the summer rush, because that's when the receptionists are drowning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more alert than scared. It's like seeing a new supermarket open on the edge of town when you run the corner shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Dr Harlow says no to bringing it forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd wait, but I'd start looking at other partnerships within an hour's drive. I'm loyal, but I'm not going to stay salaried forever in a world that's trimming salaried doctors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Harbour Lane would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our receptionist, Jean, who has three grandchildren and runs the phones like clockwork. If an AI system takes the summer calls, the partners will ask whether we need two receptionists. I'd want to find her something, maybe running the patient group.

At the partners' meeting I'd argue we should **use it well**.
think: As a **future owner**, more patients per doctor is good news.

Take the health board's **AI course** once nearby practices vouch for it.
Push for an **AI phone system** for the summer rush.
feel: **Uneasy** but alert, like a corner shop owner watching a **new supermarket** open.

fieldNote: He sees AI through a **business lens**: the owning side wins.

He'd look at **other partnerships** if loyalty to his practice doesn't pay.

steps.text: Ask Dr Harlow to bring the partnership buy-in forward a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That changes the sums completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say we need to keep a doctor responsible for every patient, and let the market sort out the rest. I'd say it to the other partners, and at church, where half the congregation are my patients and would be asking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the partnership looks like a trap. Why pay 30,000 for a share of a practice in 2028 when an AI service could offer the same care cheaper by 2029? The hands-on side, the falls and the injections, might keep a small practice going until the robots in 2031, but not at a price worth paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dr Harlow I'm holding off on the buy-in until we see what the health board does. I'd keep the 30,000 in savings instead, which would be about six months of costs for Anna and me. And we'd make the wedding smaller still, just family at the church, no hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd hate it, because I like having a plan, and this tears it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Anna that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the plan's on hold, not dead. She's a teacher, so her work changes too, but parents will still want a person in the classroom for a while. I'd probably say her job looks steadier than mine, which would be a strange thing to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said practices that use AI well do better. Doesn't that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For two years, maybe. After that, the best-run practice in town is still a practice, and the AI doesn't need a building on Harbour Lane. I believe in markets, but I don't like being on the losing side of one.

I'd say it at church, where **half the congregation** are my patients.
think: The **partnership** now looks like a trap.

Keep the **30,000** as savings, about six months of costs.
Shrink the wedding to **family at the church**, with no hall.
feel: **Anxious**, because this **tears up** the plan he relies on.
S2.quote: Why pay 30,000 for a share of a practice in 2028 when an AI service could offer the same care cheaper by 2029?
fieldNote: His free-market belief collides with being on the **losing side**.
He admits his fiancée's **teaching job** looks steadier than his.
Two years flips the buy-in from **opportunity to trap**.

steps.text: Hold off on the partnership buy-in until the health board decides

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to make a deal, if it's the right deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for practices to modernise properly, and for doctors to own the tools rather than rent them. I'd say it at the local GP meeting, quite firmly, because the practices that wait will be bought out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still buy in, but cheaper and with a way out. If I own a share from 2028, I get three years of the good part, when AI makes us more efficient, before 2031. The hands-on work, falls, dressings, injections, holds out until about 2034, so there's still something to sell even then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd negotiate the buy-in down, say 20,000 instead of 30,000, with a clause that lets me sell my share back if the health board contract changes. I'd bring in the AI note-taker and the phone system across the practice in the first year. And I'd keep 10,000 aside as a cushion and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can work with. I'd be thinking like a buyer, which I like more than thinking like a victim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Dr Harlow accept a lower price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, but he's sensible. He wants to retire with something, and fewer young doctors will want to buy a practice in this picture, so my offer might be the best one he gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the wedding, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back on as planned, church hall and all, which would make Anna's mother happy. Five years is long enough to have a wedding and still be careful with money.

The practices **that wait** will be bought out.
think: Buying in from 2028 gives me **three good years** before 2031.
**Hands-on work** holds out until about 2034, so there's still something to sell.

feel: **Uneasy** but workable, thinking like a **buyer**, not a victim.
S3.quote: I'd be thinking like a buyer, which I like more than thinking like a victim.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **renegotiate** rather than retreat.
He reasons that fewer buyers make his **lower offer** stronger.
The **wedding** goes back on, a sign he feels in control again.

steps.text: Offer 20,000 for the partnership with a sell-back clause
Bring in the AI note-taker and phone system across the practice
Keep 10,000 aside as an untouched cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to own the practice for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get this right and no reason to panic. I'd tell the younger doctors to learn a hands-on skill and learn the business side, because those last longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly calm. I'd buy in on schedule, own a share for eight years before AGI arrives, and have time to decide whether to sell or to turn Harbour Lane into something else, maybe a clinic for older people that leans on hands-on care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year is the normal plan: get ready to buy into the partnership at the agreed price, use the AI tools as the health board rolls them out, have the wedding. Once I'm in, I'd pay a bit extra off the practice loan each year, so by the mid-2030s it's nearly clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit watchful, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you sell, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If by about 2033 the health board started paying AI services directly and practices were losing patients. Then I'd sell my share while it still had value, rather than hold on out of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Anna and I want children in a few years, and ten years is long enough that I'd rather not let it decide anything. My father ran a small shop for thirty years, and he always said you plan for rain but you still plant.

Younger doctors should learn a **hands-on skill** and the **business side**.
think: Buying in on schedule gives me **eight years** of ownership before AGI.
Harbour Lane could become a **clinic for older people** focused on hands-on care.

S4.quote: My father ran a small shop for thirty years, and he always said you plan for rain but you still plant.
fieldNote: Ten years restores his **ownership plan** in full.
He has a clear **sell signal**: the health board paying AI services directly.
His father's **small-shop wisdom** shapes how he handles risk.

steps.text: Buy into the Harbour Lane partnership on schedule

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It turns the thing I've been working towards, owning part of Harbour Lane, from a good plan into a bad bet overnight. What would help is clarity from the health board about how it will pay practices in an AI world, so a young doctor knows whether buying in is sensible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who own small practices. Everyone talks about doctors losing jobs, but somebody like Dr Harlow has thirty years of his life in that building. His pension is that building.

headlineQuote: I believe in markets, but I don't like being on the losing side of one.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old salaried GP** at a three-doctor seaside practice, engaged to Anna, a teacher.
His **big plan** is to buy into the partnership when the senior partner retires.
He reads AI through a **business lens**, wanting to be on the owning side.
Fast AGI turns the buy-in into a **bad bet** and shrinks the wedding.
With more time he **negotiates** and invests, steady rather than first to move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, turning the partnership from a good plan into a bad bet.
whatWouldHelp: **Clarity** from the health board on how it will pay practices in an AI world.
